responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Second Annual Phyllis W. Meadow Award for Excellence in Psychoanalytic Writing

Jennifer Wade MSW

Jennifer Wade

Jennifer Wade   Coordinator of the Phyllis W. Meadow Award for Excellence in Psychoanalytic Writing and a licensed and certified psychoanalyst with a private practice in New York City.

With the publication of the winning papers of the second annual Phyllis W. Meadow Award for Excellence in Psychoanalytic Writing, we present work by thinkers within and outside the community of modern analysis. Our judges are impressed by thoughtful, clear, and persuasive prose that enhances our understanding of work with patients whatever the author's theoretical bent.

Our commitment to cross-pollination is reflected in the First Prize essay, “A Contract to Terminate: Mourning the End of the Transference.” Claire Kahane, a visiting scholar at the University of California and professor of English emerita at the State University of New York-Buffalo, wrote about her own analysis in this exploration of a topic infrequently examined by analytic writers.

Also presented here are the papers receiving Honorable Mention: Sharon Klayman Farber's “Autistic and Dissociative Features in Eating Disorders and Self-Mutilation,” Christopher Fowler and Andrea Celenza's “Altering Psychotic Processes: Integrated Psychoanalytic Treatment of a Schizophrenic Patient,” and Angela Sandone-Barr's “Caroline and Gold: The Study of a Fragmented Ego.

Steven Poser   Practicing psychoanalyst and a faculty member and training analyst at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies in New York City. He has contributed a number of articles and reviews to Modern Psychoanalysis. He managed John Gibson Gallery in New York City and was a consultant to the Whitney Museum, programming director of the Artists’ Television Network, and visiting critic in Drew University'sNew York Semester on Contemporary Art. An exhibiting painter since 1991, he has shown in ten one-person and eight group shows. He received the 1997 Gradiva award in painting from the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and in 1998 was visiting artist at the Boston University College of Fine Arts.

The connection between modern art and the unconscious mind is largely an untold story. The author identifies two strands in the psychoanalytic conception of the unconscious and shows how they figured in modern art from the surrealists to the abstract expressionists. He then traces a progressive repudiation of unconscious processes in the making of pop, minimal, and conceptual art.

[[RunningHead]]

Understanding Adoption: Clinical Work with Adults, Children, and Parents. K. Hushion, S. B. Sherman, and D. Siskind, eds. New York: Jason Aronson, 2006. 259 pp.

Barbara D'Amato

Barbara D'Amato

Barbara D'Amato  

Containing 15 clinical papers on psychodynamic treatment with adopted patients, this recent publication adds appreciably to the growing body of adoption literature. The editors have assembled an array of papers that not only teach novices about the prevalence and significance of adoption in the world today, but also lay important groundwork for teachers, therapists, and parents eager to gain understanding of adopted children within a variety of contexts. In accordance with current research trends, the authors collected in this volume address the specific needs of all members of the adoption triad (Javier, et al., 2007). Prominent among them is the need to work through both unconscious loss and the fantasies that accompany the more concrete, unambiguous loss experienced by all adoptees. The papers place great emphasis on the notion that loss is a necessary and normal by-product of adoption that must be worked through successfully if an adopted child is going to integrate her fantasies about birthparents with her conscious and unconscious fantasies about her adoptive parents.

In many cases adoptions occur during the preoedipal period. This fact contributes greatly to an adoptee's need to sort out thoughts and feelings about the adoption experience. Chris Bonovitz's paper, “Unconscious Communication and the Transmission of Loss,” expands on the idea first discussed by Kirk (1964) in his groundbreaking book Shared Fate that emphasizes the feelings of loss shared by adopted child and adoptive parents. Both writers suggest that it is through this shared loss that each can connect with the other. Through their “intermingling loss,” parent and child can be healed by the new experience of becoming a family (p. 18). Bonovitz also addresses the potential for an “intergenerational transmission of trauma,” in which loss of a family member within the adoptive family may impact the experiences of the adopted child who may become the recipient of wishes to deny or to act as a replacement for that loss. Unconscious fantasy about loss, then, is another necessary aspect of adoption that is not pathological, yet can lead to difficulties when it remains unresolved.

responseSet.title: Hyman Spotnitz: The Editors
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Hyman Spotnitz

The Editors

Hyman Spotnitz died on April 18, 2008, just short of the one-hundredth anniversary of his birth. This is the first issue in the history of this journal in which his name does not appear as a member of the board of consultants. The term modern psychoanalysis for the body of theory this publication was founded to explore and develop was Spotnitz's term; he titled the definitive statement of his theory of technique Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient. He published that book in 1969, nearly 30 years into his work toward the development of what must by now be termed a school of thought, providing as it does the intellectual foundation of this journal and several professional training centers and academic institutions.

The loss over the last three years of our primary sources of inspiration—not only Spotnitz, but the founding editor of this journal, Phyllis W. Meadow, in 2005—prompts us to undertake to consolidate our intellectual resources as we press on. In assembling this issue we came to ask ourselves some interesting questions, among them: What are the intellectual origins of modern psychoanalysis? Will an answer to that question help us to determine the place of modern psychoanalysis in the larger discipline? and Shall we be concerned with placing ourselves in that framework today? These concerns are secondary to the clinical questions this journal is charged with exploring, but they are not insignificant to our practice with patients, and we believe they have been and will continue to be worth our attention.

The Use of Modern Psychoanalytic Techniques in the Treatment of Children and Adolescents**

Robert Quackenbush PHD LCSW

Robert Quackenbush

460 East 79th Street
New York, NY 10075
rqstudios@aol.com

Robert Quackenbush   Has specialized in working with children for many years as a psychoanalyst/psychotherapist and educator in private practice. He is author and illustrator of more than 200 books for young readers, both fiction and nonfiction.

The author describes how he uses modern psychoanalytic techniques in his work with children as a psychoanalyst, teacher of art, and author/illustrator of children's books. Case examples illustrate how children and adolescents communicate in symbolic language the hidden thoughts and feelings that they cannot consciously comprehend or that they fear will be rejected by their parents, teachers, and other caretakers. The author discusses how play and art therapy techniques are used to gain understanding of each symbolic communication in order to help children and adolescents put their thoughts and feelings into words and remove the emotional blocks that prevent them from realizing their full potential.

[[RunningHead]]

False Self: The Life of Masud Khan. L. Hopkins. New York: Other Press, 2006. 295 pp.

Stephen Guttman

Stephen Guttman

Stephen Guttman  

Linda Hopkins, the author of this fascinating and troubling biography, trained as an analyst at the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis, a modern Freudian institute devoted to the work of Hyman Spotnitz where she is now a training analyst and supervisor. She explains her interest in Masud Khan as developing partly out of her undergraduate studies in Arabic and Islam, but mainly from her later studies at the Washington School of Psychoanalysis (now the International Psychotherapy Institute in Bethesda, Maryland), an institute oriented toward British psychoanalysis.

Masud Khan (1924-1989) was a tremendously influential psychoanalytic thinker and charismatic figure who had a huge impact on the development of British psychoanalysis, and psychoanalysis in general, after World War II. His first three books [The Privacy of the Self: Papers on Psychoanalytic Theory and Technique (1974), Alienation in Perversions (1979), and Hidden Selves: Between Theory and Practice in Psychoanalysis (1983)] are considered major contributions to psychoanalysis though his work as Winnicott's editor—which probably included much of the actual writing of works like Through Pœdiatrics to Psycho-Analysis—makes him a central figure in the development of psychoanalytic thought in the 1950s and ‘60s. He was also widely considered to be a brilliant, if eccentric, clinician.

Hopkins opens her book with a quote from Khan's one-time friend André Green: “No one can deny Masud's talent. But it is also impossible to deny his sickness and his evil nature. When you have met someone like him, you know that the mind is not simple” (p. xix).

From the Couch to the Circle: Hyman Spotnitz and Group Psychotherapy

Leslie Rosenthal PHD

Leslie Rosenthal

12 West 96th Street
New York, NY 10025

Leslie Rosenthal   Dean emeritus of group studies at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He has served as group therapy consultant in a wide variety of clinical and educational settings, including the Jewish Board of Guardians from 1956 to 1975 and the department of psychiatry at Jacobi Medical Center and at Montefiore Hospital. In 2007, he received the Gradiva award from N.A.A.P. for two papers: “The New Member: ‘Infanticide’ in Group Therapy” and “The Thermostatic Function of the Group Analyst: Regulating the Degree of Stimulation in the Group.” He has written extensively on various aspects of the group psychotherapy experience, with a focus on the various tasks of the group therapist, and is a life fellow of the American Group Psychotherapy Association.

This paper considers Spotnitz as a group psychoanalyst and examines the important contributions he made to this developing field at both a clinical and a theoretical level. The author demonstrates Spotnitz's effectiveness as a group leader through examples of his insightful emotional communications with group members.

Andrea Celenza   Assistant clinical professor at Harvard Medical School and a faculty member of the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute and of the Massachusetts Institute of Psychoanalysis. She has written and presented numerous papers on the evaluation and treatment of therapists who have engaged in sexual misconduct with a focus on training and supervisory issues. In 2006 she was the recipient of the Karl A. She is in private practice in Lexington, MA.

This paper explores the differential effects of the integrated psychody-namic treatment of a schizophrenic woman. In the initial stage of treatment, supportive interventions including hospitalizations, social skills training, and holding functions were supplied by a day-treatment program, and supportive/expressive interventions to contain anxiety and overstimulation were provided by the therapist. Later in treatment, more extensive expressive interventions were introduced to correspond maximally to the patient's level of functioning. A core psychoanalytic intervention targeted specific hallucinations as expressions of unmodulated affective experiences, while the day-treatment program focused on impulse control and coping skills. The treatment approach resulted in significant improvement in the patient's quality of life and led to fewer suicide attempts and a reduction in the medical cost associated with those attempts.

Psychoanalysis and the “Cognitive Unconscious”: Implications for Clinical Technique

Dan Gilhooley Psy.D.

Dan Gilhooley

25 East 10 Street, 1F
New York, NY 10003
dangilhooley@yahoo.com

Dan Gilhooley   Licensed psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and Bellport, NY. He is a faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) and a graduate of CMPS, the Boston Graduate School for Psychoanalysis, and the C. Z. Meadow Institute. In 2007 Dr. Gilhooley was a research fellow in the psychoanalytic research training program jointly sponsored by the Anna Freud Centre and the Yale Child Study Center. A visual artist with 18 one-person exhibitions, he was elected to the National Academy of Design in 1991. In 1995 he received a Gradiva Award for Art Advancing Psychoanalysis from the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis.

Recent empirical research from the field of cognitive science in the areas of perception, memory, learning, intuition, decision making, and motivation suggests a radical reconception of mental life, in which the role and scope of the unconscious is vastly increased and the role of consciousness is correspondingly reduced. Many of these empirical findings support the psychoanalytic conception of the centrality of unconscious processes in guiding behavior. However, if this radical reconception proposed by cognitive science is true, it suggests that psychoanalysis may need to revise its conception of insight in therapeutic action and reconsider aspects of clinical technique such as anonymity, action, and emotional communication. It is proposed that reverie and mutual regression are unconscious states that could be empirically investigated.

This paper explores the meaning of self-harm behavior and the treatment of patients who engage in it. Vulnerable individuals can derive a feeling of power and omnipotence from cutting, burning, or starving themselves or engaging in bulimic purging or other self-harm. The case of a woman with a long history of self-mutilation is presented, in which autistic and dissociative elements are paramount. Like the autistic child who fears she is at the brink of falling into madness, the self-harmer throws herself into madness, merging the boundaries between self and other in a dedifferentiated, dissociated state. Inflicting pain and injury on oneself is a protective mechanism that can arise when one experiences the terror of feeling alone and helpless, at the mercy of predators. Having lacked the ability to develop transitional objects for self-soothing, self-harmers instead prey upon themselves with hard autistic objects, a perverse form of self-soothing. In comparing the dissociative and autistic features of self-harm, the paper raises questions about the relationship between autistic and dissociative processes and their relationship to psychoses.

Rodrigo Barahona  

Dany Nobus and Lisa Downing's (2006) Perversion: Psychoanalytic Perspectives/Perspectives on Psychoanalysis constitutes an important and provocative contribution to the literature in psychoanalysis as well as the humanities. The first half of the book is devoted to psychoanalysts’ clinical and theoretical material, while the second half features scholars from the humanities considering the social and cultural repercussions of psychoanalytic rhetoric and their ideas on how to move forward. The two sections of the book are introduced by short essays from Nobus and Downing, respectively.

Nobus masterfully and humorously describes to the reader the polemic justifying a volume of collected essays like this one, beginning with a deceptively simple question:

Why is using a plumed feather for sexual purposes regarded as “healthy,” “normal,” and “erotic,” whereas employing a whole bird is unequivocally considered “sick,” “bizarre,” “abnormal,” “deviant,” and “pathological?” (P-3)

With this, Nobus sets the tone for the articles to come.

Angela Musolino  

George Makari has written a very readable history of the creation and evolution of psychoanalysis until the mid-1940s. Revolution in Mind: The Creation of Psychoanalysis presents a satisfying scientific summary and occasionally shocking revelation of the human brilliance and foibles that are the matrix of psychoanalytic theory, practice, and technique.

Makari begins in France at the time that Freud arrived to undertake his studies with Charcot—placing Freud squarely in the context of the intellectual and political crucible of the latter half of the 19th century. Making a quick tour through scientific rationalism, psychologie nouvelle, associational psychology, Auguste Comte's positivism, Th$eAodule Ribot's studies in heredity and its relationship to psychological functioning, and Jean-Martin Charcot's studies in neurology and hysteria, Makari reveals that Paris was a Mecca for anyone interested in exploring the questions of the human mind. He detours briefly to Vienna and the educational and ideational influences Freud had been exposed to there. Sketching the sociopolitical landscape of Europe in the latter half of the 19th century, where scientific rationalism was rising as the religious authority was fading in the context of a new political and social force in France, Freud is revealed as a man embedded in a particular time and place, and steeped in the intellectual and scientific traditions and controversies of that time.

103
